嗣.meaning: The old <part>director</part> of a puppet theatre retires. Instead of passing his plays to his son, he tucks the <part>scroll</part> of every script into the wooden <part>mouth</part> of his favourite puppet, a grumpy owl. The owl clacks its beak and takes a bow: the theatre's new <kanji>heir</kanji>.
嗣.on: On opening night the owl hides behind a painted <sound>shi</sound>eld and recites every line from memory.

恣.meaning: At the ice cream van, the girl at the window calls '<part>next</part>!', but the man at the front never moves. He just orders another scoop for himself, then another, until he holds a tower topped with a cone shaped like a <part>heart</part>, all his. The whole queue groans: how <kanji>selfish</kanji>.
恣.on: When a little dog begs for a lick, he blocks the cone with a knight's <sound>shi</sound>eld.
恣.kun: Then he grabs a <sound>ho</sound>tdog, wraps up in a <sound>shee</sound>pskin rug and slurps two <sound>mu</sound>gs of <sound>mu</sound>lled cider, all just as he pleases.

壱.meaning: A <part>gentleman</part> in a top hat goes camping with exactly one thing: a silver <part>spoon</part>, which he tucks under a tiny <part>blanket</part> each night. Asked how many spoons he packed, he lifts one gloved finger and answers in his poshest voice: 'Precisely one.' That's <kanji>one (formal)</kanji>.
壱.on: At sunrise he paints the spoon on an <sound>ea</sound>sel, while a curious <sound>chee</sound>tah peeks at the lonely canvas.
壱.kun: He sleeps with his <sound>hee</sound>ls against a <sound>to</sound>tem pole, then wakes and sneezes once, very politely: '<sound>Tsu</sound>!'

訃.meaning: The town's oldest <part>faucet</part> drips its last drop after a hundred years. The mayor gives a teary <part>speech</part> beside it, and next morning the paper prints half a page about its long, leaky life, with a photo of it in its prime: the faucet's <kanji>obituary</kanji>.
訃.on: Its worn-out washer is laid to rest on a tiny rolled-up <sound>fu</sound>ton.
訃.kun: The paper girl reads it, and <sound>she</sound> <sound>ru</sound>shes off to <sound>se</sound>nd the sad news to every door on the street.

畏.meaning: Over a <part>rice field</part>, a <part>garment</part> floats up all by itself: a huge golden robe, arms spread wide, with <part>one</part> stiff belt across its middle. The frogs stop croaking, the farmer drops his hoe, and the whole valley stares up, speechless with <kanji>awe</kanji>.
畏.on: Even an <sound>ee</sound>l pokes its head out of the mud to gape at it.
畏.kun: A <sound>ca</sound>lm <sound>shee</sound>pdog bows low before the robe, a <sound>co</sound>conut balanced on its head: respectfully.

附.meaning: A goat on a mountain keeps eating every flag the climbers plant. So the last climber finds a way to <part>attach</part> her <part>pennant</part> to the goat's own horn with tape, glue and three knots. Now the summit flag wanders the mountain all day, firmly <kanji>affixed</kanji>.
附.on: At night the goat curls up on a rolled-out <sound>fu</sound>ton, the flag still waving over its head.
附.kun: A <sound>tsu</sound>nami of wind roars up the slope, and the flag still clings on.

但.meaning: A hotel hangs a sign on the <part>coat hook</part> by the door: 'Free breakfast for all!' Below, in tiny letters: 'Served only before <part>daybreak</part>.' Guests stagger down at four in their pyjamas, grumbling about that one little <kanji>however</kanji>.
但.on: The kitchen is reached through a long, dark <sound>tun</sound>nel, so they bump into each other with their trays.
但.kun: At the end, a <sound>tu</sound>gboat captain, a <sound>du</sound>ck and a <sound>shee</sound>p have already eaten everything. They read the small print first.

煎.meaning: A penguin chef stands <part>in front</part> of a grill of glowing <part>hot coals</part>, flipping fish with his flippers. He keeps leaning closer for a better look, until his own bow tie starts to smoke. He's learning the hard way how to <kanji>broil</kanji>.
煎.on: A <sound>sen</sound>try walrus stands by with a bucket of snow in case the chef catches fire.
煎.kun: After dinner the penguin boils seaweed into a dark, bitter brew and sells it for one <sound>cen</sound>t a cup: to brew by boiling.

哺.meaning: A mother hedgehog lies in the barn while her babies drink, each tiny <part>mouth</part> busy. The farmer's cat stands guard with a <part>flyswatter</part>, whacking every fly that buzzes near. Nobody disturbs a hedgehog while she's trying to <kanji>nurse</kanji>.
哺.on: When the babies finally sleep, the cat rewards itself with a <sound>ho</sound>tdog.
哺.kun: Years later the grown hedgehogs give the cat a <sound>hug</sound> and a <sound>cu</sound>shion of soft hay: it helped raise them.

且.meaning: A pushy peddler on a night train holds up a lamp shaped like the <part>moon</part>. 'It glows! It hums!' Then he always has <part>one</part> more thing to add: a stand, a spare bulb, a free bag. Nobody needs them, but nobody can say no to his favourite word, <kanji>moreover</kanji>.
且.on: He sells it all from a tiny <sound>sho</sound>p in the last carriage, so short a stop the doors slam shut mid-sale.
且.kun: And he throws in a free <sound>cu</sound>p of tea as well.

𠮟.meaning: Every morning at <part>seven</part>, a cuckoo bursts out of the clock in the hall, opens its little wooden <part>mouth</part> and yells at the family: shoes on the stairs! Crumbs on the table! Even the dog gets told off. This clock doesn't cuckoo, it likes to <kanji>scold</kanji>.
𠮟.on: The family hides under a big bed <sound>sheet</sound>, but it shouts through that too.
𠮟.kun: Then Grandma scolds it right back: <sound>she</sound> <sound>cu</sound>ts it off mid-squawk with one firm 'Enough!'

弐.meaning: A butler sets up a croquet lawn, hammering in a <part>stake</part> and laying <part>two</part> polished mallets beside it. 'How many players, madam?' The duchess raises two gloved fingers: 'Two, if you please.' That is <kanji>two (formal)</kanji>.
弐.on: She keeps score by poking tiny holes in a card with a <sound>nee</sound>dle.
弐.kun: Between shots, the duchess cools one <sound>foo</sound>t in a <sound>tu</sound>b of iced tea.

冶.meaning: A tiny blacksmith mouse sets a thimble of tin on a stone <part>pedestal</part> over her candle and watches it glow and run like honey. Then she pours it into a mould packed in <part>ice</part>, where it hisses into a tiny sword. Her favourite part is the <kanji>melting</kanji>.
冶.on: She wraps the warm hilt in a scrap of <sound>ya</sound>rn so she can hold it.
冶.kun: '<sound>Ee</sound>k!' she squeaks when a hot drop splashes her tail, and carries on casting.

沃.meaning: A garden gnome in a <part>tilted hat</part> catches <part>water drops</part> in its brim every night and tips them onto the soil at dawn. Soon its patch grows pumpkins the size of cars and carrots taller than the shed. No soil in town can match its <kanji>fertility</kanji>.
沃.on: One morning a <sound>yo</sound>-yo dropped in the patch sprouts into a whole yo-yo bush.
沃.kun: So the neighbours pour water over an old <sound>so</sound>fa and a lost <sound>so</sound>ck on the lawn, hoping they sprout too.

苛.meaning: A gardener trims her <part>grass</part> blade by blade with nail scissors, desperate for the show judge's <part>approval</part>. Every year he squints and says, 'One blade is crooked.' Every year she trims again. Ten years of that one crooked blade: pure <kanji>torment</kanji>.
苛.on: She shows him her pond, hoping a big orange <sound>ca</sound>rp will cheer him up. It splashes his clipboard.
苛.kun: '<sound>Ea</sound>sy!' he tells her, then drives off in his <sound>jee</sound>p, right across her lawn: what a bully.

采.meaning: Under an old <part>tree</part>, a raccoon runs a midnight game. With one <part>claw</part> it scoops up two little cubes, shakes them and rolls them across a root. The squirrels gasp: double six again. Nobody ever beats the raccoon's lucky <kanji>dice</kanji>.
采.on: The winner gets a jug of apple <sound>ci</sound>der, and it's always the raccoon.
采.kun: Then it takes all the acorns and stacks them behind a <sound>to</sound>tem pole.

咽.meaning: An opera hippo opens her huge <part>mouth</part> for the high note, and nothing comes out but a squeak. The doctor peers in with a torch and finds the <part>cause</part>: a ping-pong ball stuck halfway down her <kanji>throat</kanji>.
咽.on: He fishes it out stained blue: she had gargled <sound>in</sound>k by mistake.
咽.kun: In the front row, a <sound>moo</sound>se laughs so hard it chokes and splutters all over the <sound>se</sound>at in front.

剝.meaning: A sticker of a smiling sun has been stuck on the town <part>fountain</part> for years. The caretaker warms it with an <part>iron</part>, slides a blunt little <part>dagger</part> under one corner and pulls. With a long, happy rip, the whole sticker starts to <kanji>come off</kanji>.
剝.on: Underneath, someone long ago painted a purple <sound>huck</sound>leberry.
剝.kun: A <sound>he</sound>n hops up and pecks away the last flakes of glue: stripped clean.

朕.meaning: An <part>alien</part> lands on the <part>moon</part>, plants a flag and crowns himself king of all the craters. From then on he never says 'I': 'We are hungry', 'We shall nap now', though he's the only one there. He speaks in the <kanji>imperial we</kanji>.
朕.on: He strokes his long green <sound>chin</sound> and announces, 'We approve.'

淫.meaning: A sailor's parrot perches on a <part>spindle</part> by the dock, dipping one <part>claw</part> in the <part>water drops</part>, and screeches rude rhymes at every passing boat. The vicar covers his ears and the ladies row faster. That bird is the harbour's one source of <kanji>lewdness</kanji>.
淫.on: The vicar blacks out the rhymes it reads off the dock wall with a pot of <sound>in</sound>k.
淫.kun: '<sound>Hee</sound>-hee,' cackles the parrot, as the vicar soaks his brush in a <sound>tu</sound>b of soapy water: to soak.

羞.meaning: A <part>sheep</part> sneaks into the barn, grabs a <part>C-clamp</part> and tries to fix the fence it broke. One wild <part>slash</part> of the clamp, and the whole fence falls flat just as the farmer walks in. The sheep hides its face in its wool: it can only <kanji>feel ashamed</kanji>.
羞.on: It tries to hide behind the farmer's giant muddy <sound>shoe</sound>.
羞.kun: <sound>Hu</sound>mbled, it climbs into the farmer's <sound>jee</sound>p and hides under a sack.

舷.meaning: A cat crosses the harbour by walking the top edge of a rowing <part>boat</part> like a tightrope, while a fisherman reels in his line on a squeaky <part>spool</part>. Each time the boat rocks, the cat grips that narrow wooden rim tighter: the <kanji>gunwale</kanji>.
舷.on: 'Steady, <sound>Gen</sound>!' the fisherman calls to the cat, whose name is Gen.
舷.kun: The fisherman's <sound>foo</sound>t knocks a bag of <sound>nu</sound>ts and a <sound>bu</sound>tter <sound>tu</sound>b along the rim.

僅.meaning: A giant hangs his coat on a <part>coat hook</part> nailed to a hill and sits down to a feast. He opens his huge <part>mouth</part>, but his plate holds just one blade of <part>grass</part> and one crumb of <part>soil</part>. It's hard to fill a giant with a meal so <kanji>slight</kanji>.
僅.on: A <sound>kin</sound>gfisher drops him a minnow, which doesn't help much.
僅.kun: He stares in <sound>wo</sound>nder at dessert: one drop of yu<sound>zu</sound> juice.

塡.meaning: A dog digs forty holes in the lawn before its owner gets home. In a panic it grabs a <part>spoon</part> and every garden <part>tool</part> it can drag, and shovels the <part>soil</part> back as fast as its paws allow. When the door opens, it sits wagging, having raced to <kanji>fill in</kanji> every last hole.
塡.on: Next door, a <sound>ten</sound>or leans out of the window and sings it a victory song.
塡.kun: <sound>Hu</sound>ffing, it pushes its nose into the last <sound>mu</sound>d hole, and it fits perfectly: stuck tight.

慄.meaning: A cowboy camps under a lone <part>tree</part> out <part>west</part>. At midnight the branches creak and whisper, his <part>heartbeat</part> drums in his ears and his teeth chatter. In the morning it turns out to be a goat chewing the bark, but it was a long night's <kanji>shiver</kanji>.
慄.on: He calms his nerves by nibbling a whole box of <sound>Ritz</sound> crackers.
慄.kun: He trembles under his <sound>fu</sound>ton while a <sound>roo</sound>k laughs at him from the branch.

虞.meaning: At the zoo gift shop, a <part>tiger</part> in a bow tie holds out a box and purrs, 'I <part>give</part> this to you.' The box is ticking. Your hand hovers over it: a gift, or a trick? You reach out slowly, full of <kanji>apprehension</kanji>.
虞.on: Inside is only a small <sound>goo</sound>die bag, rattling with sweets.
虞.kun: You tip it out: a jelly <sound>o</sound>ctopus, a tiny <sound>so</sound>fa and a <sound>re</sound>d note that says 'BOO'.

詣.meaning: A snail sets off when the town announces a picnic, crawling for a whole year towards the smell of something <part>delicious</part>. It reaches the park just as the mayor ends his closing <part>speech</part> and everyone is packing up. Still, the snail is proud: it did <kanji>arrive</kanji>.
詣.on: One slice of <sound>ca</sound>ke has been saved, just for it.
詣.kun: The snail bows to the mayor, its shell trailing behind like a royal <sound>ca</sound>pe: a polite visit.

遡.meaning: A gardener's <part>moonflower</part> only blooms where its river begins. So each night she sets it in a little boat and hauls it up a wooden <part>ramp</part> beside every waterfall, against the current, mile after mile. She and her flower <kanji>go upstream</kanji>.
遡.on: At the top she sleeps on a squashy <sound>so</sound>fa she has dragged along too.
遡.kun: At <sound>su</sound>nset a fish tips her <sound>cu</sound>p of tea overboard. '<sound>No</sound>!' she cries, then rows on past a <sound>bo</sound>nsai growing on a rock.

辣.meaning: A florist mixes up her orders and ties a <part>chili</part> into every wedding <part>bundle</part> instead of a rose. At the ceremony the bride sniffs her bouquet, and the whole front row starts coughing and weeping. Lovely flowers, but very <kanji>pungent</kanji>.
辣.on: The couple's car speeds off down a lane full of <sound>ruts</sound>, everyone inside still sneezing.
辣.kun: One guest bites a chili, gulps a <sound>cu</sound>p of punch and <sound>ru</sound>ns for the fountain.

憬.meaning: A goldfish in an office bowl stares at a postcard of mountain <part>scenery</part> taped to the glass. Each time it looks, its <part>heartbeat</part> flutters and it swims in slow, sad circles. It has never seen a mountain, but it can't help but <kanji>yearn for</kanji> one.
憬.on: Every birthday it wishes for those peaks over a fish-food <sound>ca</sound>ke.
憬.kun: '<sound>Ah</sound>,' it sighs, dreaming of a <sound>ko</sound>ala on a snowy peak, and <sound>gu</sound>lps a bubble.
